evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 3.1.7: nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō
terms.comment: Of people and of things (rūs amat, Ov. Met. 14.627). In comedy and Cicero’s letters amō tē also thanks (Meritō tē amō, Ter. Ad. 945–946), and amābō is “please” (see please).

evidence: Cic. Off. 1.12: praecipuum quendam amōrem in eōs quī prōcreātī sunt
terms.comment: Also of the one loved: dēliciīs atque amōribus meīs (Cic. Att. 16.6.4).

evidence: Catull. 72.4: sed pater ut gnātōs dīligit et generōs
Traupman 98: to be fond of, dīligō
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to value or esteem highly, to love”: the love of regard and choice, as of a father for his children in Catullus.
Loving and affectionate, often with the genitive and in the superlative: amantissimus tuī, most devoted to you.

terms.gloss: be madly in love with, be dying of love for
terms.grammar: verb, irregular, like pereō; with the accusative of the person loved, often with amōre
terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut.; nōn apud Cic., Verg., Hor., Ov.
evidence: Plaut. Epid. 2.2.35: illa, quam tuus gnātus annōs multōs deamat, dēperit (Lewis & Short s.v. deamō)
Plaut. Cist. 1.3.43: is amōre prōjectīciam illam dēperit (Lewis & Short s.v. amor)
Traupman 103: to be mad about, dēpereō (+ acc.)
terms.comment: Literally “to perish (for someone)”. The person is in the accusative, as the object of the passion: illam dēperit, he is crazy about her. Lewis & Short: frequent in Plautus, not in Cicero, Virgil, Horace or Ovid.

terms.gloss: to love desperately, be infatuated with
evidence: Plaut. Am. 1.3.19: ut hic tē efflictim dēperit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Efflictim, “to death, desperately”, goes with amāre and dēperīre.

phrases.latin: nōn enim concēdō tibi plūs ut illum amēs quam ipse amō
phrases.english: For I won’t grant that you love him more than I do.
My dear Geta, I love you all.

phrases.latin: dīlēxī tum tē nōn tantum ut vulgus amīcam, sed pater ut gnātōs dīligit et generōs
phrases.english: I loved you then not just as the crowd loves a girlfriend, but as a father loves his sons and sons-in-law.

phrases.latin: nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē: hoc tantum possum dīcere, nōn amō tē
phrases.english: I don’t love you, Sabidius, and I can’t say why; all I can say is this: I don’t love you.
